mappings.note: Statements 1 and 3 are the sign/origin convention for one-dimensional motion and statement 2 is the distance-equals-displacement condition - all three sit in LO-1's 'for objects moving in a straight line' differentiation clause. Nothing is plotted or computed.

Turn-back numbers (0 to 100 to 40 m) with both distance and displacement demanded: the distinction is the whole answer. Not LO-2 despite the timestamps - no graph is supplied and no rate is asked for.
Identical demand to its O6 sibling stated without times: path length 160 m against net 40 m. LO-1's differentiation clause; LO-4 is excluded because no kinematic equation is involved.

Labelling which vector is velocity and which acceleration for a braking car probes the definition of acceleration and its direction relative to velocity in straight-line motion - LO-1. No value is produced, so LO-2/LO-4 do not apply.
Asks directly which statement correctly differentiates distance from displacement (|s| can never exceed path length). The most literal reading of LO-1's first clause in the chapter.
Recall of the defining formula for average speed. LO-1 defines the quantity; LO-4 would require given values to substitute, and none are given.

Assertion-reason contrasting the sign-bearing nature of average velocity with the magnitude-only nature of average speed - the speed/velocity differentiation in LO-1, tested on the vector/scalar property rather than on numbers.
The equality condition for |average velocity| and average speed. Same LO-1 clause as its P5 and V73 siblings; distinguished only by being posed as a four-option choice.
Uniform vs non-uniform motion defined by equal/unequal distances in equal times - LO-1's constant-velocity description of straight-line motion. No graph is involved, so the LO-2 sibling is out.

A data table, not a graph: the conclusion to select is that displacement returns to zero while distance keeps growing. LO-1's differentiation; LO-2 is excluded because nothing is read from a plotted axis.

POOR FIT. The recall target is the name of a 5th-century treatise, not any kinematic outcome. Cited to LO-1 because the concept the treatise is invoked for is the definition of speed; the history-of-science content itself has no home in this frame.
Length-and-back in a pool gives zero displacement hence zero average velocity. The number 0 falls out of the distinction, not out of an equation, so LO-1 rather than LO-4.
Ordering the three steps of the defining operation for average acceleration. No values are supplied, so this tests the definition (LO-1) rather than a calculation from given quantities (LO-4).
Naming the quantity that is the rate of change of velocity: LO-1's 'define ... acceleration' clause in its barest form.

The conclusion to pick names a kinematic quantity extracted from the position-time graph - B's steeper slope means higher velocity. Slope of position-time giving velocity is LO-2's named operation, which separates it from the LO-1 graph items where the answer is a state of motion.
Acceleration opposite to velocity means decreasing speed - the direction half of LO-1's definition of acceleration. No graph and no numbers, so it splits from its LO-2 and LO-4 siblings.
Given u=0, v=20, t=10, produce a number. Splits from the definitional acceleration items (O17, O18) precisely because values are supplied and an unknown is solved for.

Free fall: acceleration constant and downward. LO-1 supplies 'define acceleration', but the actual content is acceleration due to gravity, which is named only at competency level (C2.1) and by no learning outcome - hence the second, broader code.
High velocity with zero acceleration: tests that acceleration is defined by the rate of change, not the magnitude, of velocity. LO-1's definitional clause; nothing to calculate or graph.
Four-row table: pick the car whose initial and final positions coincide. The discriminator is displacement vs path length, so LO-1, not LO-2 (a table is not a graph) and not LO-4 (no equation).
Graph-construction convention (time on the x-axis). Sits in LO-1's 'plot ... position-time and velocity-time graphs' clause; LO-2 is excluded because no quantity is being taken off a graph.

Constant speed on a circular path is still accelerated motion - LO-1's 'define ... uniform circular motion'. C-8.1-LO-2 is reserved for the 2(pi)R/T speed expression, which this question does not touch.

A line parallel to the time axis on a position-time graph means the object is stationary. What is read off is a state of motion, not a kinematic quantity, which is the line that separates this from its LO-2 siblings.
Inclined straight line through the origin means constant velocity. Again a state of motion read from graph shape (LO-1's interpret clause), not a value obtained from the slope (LO-2).

The two true statements (slope gives average velocity; steeper means greater velocity) are LO-2's slope-of-position-time operation; the false statement about a curved line is decided by LO-1's shape-to-motion reading. Both are needed to answer.
